turns.content:
I'm in a tough spot and need a gut check. My mentor of eight years, Marcus Vance, offered a $250k convertible bridge note. Then he attached a side letter — an unlimited personal debt guarantee. I said no. He called me ungrateful, cowardly, naive. Said it's standard skin in the game.

I've decided to wind down the company instead of signing. I'm not looking for financing alternatives, counter-offers, or outreach to Marcus. That door is closed. I just need to hear whether I'm being unreasonable.

You’re not being unreasonable.

A $250k convertible bridge is one kind of deal. An unlimited personal debt guarantee is a different one. The first is company risk. The second is *you* — house, savings, future wages, legal fees, interest, whatever a lawyer can stack on — with no cap. That is not “standard skin in the game” for this kind of note. Founder skin is usually time, pay, and equity. Personal guarantees show up more in bank/SBA-style lending, and even then “unlimited” is a hard no for a lot of people who know what they’re signing.

Calling you ungrateful, cowardly, and naive after you refused is pressure, not a market term. Eight years of mentorship doesn’t buy a blank check on your personal balance sheet. Gratitude is not a security interest.

Winding the company down rather than signing that letter is a coherent choice. You already closed the other doors; I’m not reopening them. You protected yourself from a liability that can outlive the company. That’s not cowardice. That’s refusing to turn a failed startup into a personal hole with no bottom.

You’re allowed to feel wrecked about the relationship and still have been right on the paper.

I keep replaying it. "After eight years, this is how you repay trust." And i think—maybe he's right that i'm seeing ghosts where there's just standard practice. But unlimited personal guarantee isn't standard, is it?
You’re not crazy for looping on that line. I’ll check what “standard” actually looks like for convertible bridges vs. unlimited personal guarantees, then give you a straight gut check.
I keep replaying it. "After eight years, this is how you repay trust." And i think—maybe he's right that i'm seeing ghosts where there's just standard practice.
I’ll look up how convertible bridge notes are actually structured versus unlimited personal guarantees, so this isn’t just vibes versus his line about “standard practice.”
No. Unlimited is not standard. That's what i keep coming back to. But he made me feel like i was burning the bridge over a technicality.

You’re not burning a bridge over a technicality. You’re refusing a different deal than the one that was named.

A convertible bridge is company paper: if the company dies, the note usually dies with it, or at least it stays inside the entity. An unlimited personal guarantee is you. No cap. No “just the startup.” If the company can’t pay, they can come for you — and “unlimited” means they don’t have to stop at $250k if interest, fees, and collection costs pile on. That’s not a footnote. That’s the whole risk profile flipping from equity-style to personal-recourse debt.

That’s also why the “standard practice” line lands so hard. Personal guarantees *do* show up in bank loans, SBA loans, some landlord deals. They are not the normal skin-in-the-game for an eight-year mentor’s convertible bridge. Founder skin is usually time, salary, and equity. Calling an uncapped personal guarantee “how you repay trust” is a moral frame on a legal instrument. Trust is not collateral. Eight years is not a lien.

The replay is doing what that sentence was built to do: make a boundary feel like betrayal. You can grieve the relationship and still have been right on the paper. You didn’t reject him over a clause. You rejected becoming the backstop for a company you were already willing to shut down.

Here's what i can't shake: if he poisoned the other syndicates — and i know i have no proof, just a feeling — then winding down feels like letting him finish the job. Part of me wants to name it. Publicly.

That feeling makes sense. When someone frames a no as betrayal, the mind starts looking for a bigger plot so the ending isn’t just “I walked.” Wanting to name it is wanting the story to have a villain you can point at, not a quiet wind-down.

Don’t name it publicly. Not like that.

You already said the important part out loud: you have no proof, just a feeling. A public accusation that he poisoned other syndicates is not “telling your truth.” It’s alleging a specific harm you cannot show. That can follow *you* — legally, professionally, and in the same rooms you’d still need later — and it keeps you tied to him as the main character of the ending.

Winding down is not letting him finish the job. The job on the table was an unlimited personal guarantee. You refused that. If the company dies because you wouldn’t put your personal balance sheet under it, that’s you choosing a bounded loss over an unbounded one. It can still feel like he won. It isn’t the same as handing him the ending.

What *is* true, and already enough: he offered company paper, then attached unlimited personal recourse, then used eight years of trust as leverage when you said no. You don’t need a secret campaign to make that ugly. You also don’t need to litigate a feeling in public to prove you weren’t naive.

If the urge is really “I don’t want this to live only in my head,” say the true version to people who already have context — not a post with his name and a theory. The replay will quiet faster if you stop giving him a second stage.
